sources.title: NPR Topics: Home Page Top Stories

articles.author: Larry Kaplow
articles.description: The novel proposal would have charged billionaires a one-time 5% tax on most of their overall wealth, including their ownership in companies.
articles.title: California voters defeat billionaire tax proposal that divided Democrats

articles.author: Jenna McLaughlin
articles.description: France says Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites last month, turning up temperatures in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.
articles.title: France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks

articles.author: Becky Sullivan
articles.description: The College Football Playoff is expanding again. The 12-team format lasted just three years. Starting next fall, the field will expand to 24 teams in a massive moment of transformation for the sport.
articles.title: College Football Playoff will expand to 24 teams in another sea change for the sport

articles.author: Hadeel Al-Shalchi
articles.description: Thousands of diplomats, executives and leaders are gathering in Turkey for a global climate summit. In recent years, Turkey has moved to be more eco-conscious, but some say that hasn't been enough.
articles.title: Turkey hosts world climate summit, but some critics accuse it of 'greenwashing'

articles.author: Andrew Limbong
articles.description: M. John Harrison's slim novel is the first Booker Prize winner that's "emerged from the bona fide [sci-fi] world," according to the Booker Prize Foundation's chief executive.
articles.title: Apocalyptic sci-fi novel 'The End of Everything' wins this year's Booker Prize

articles.author: Carlos Morales
articles.description: The Trump administration filed an emergency relief request with the high court earlier in October asking for the construction to continue while a lawsuit over the plan moves forward.
articles.title: Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in west Texas

articles.author: Barbara Sprunt
articles.description: The articles accuse Hegseth of "high crimes and misdemeanors," including for waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution.
articles.title: Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth

articles.author: Maureen Corrigan
articles.description: Both Poe and Doyle have generated mountains of literary criticism over the years, but Darkness Becomes Bright and Sleuth-Hound remind us there's a lot left to discover about these masters.
articles.title: We are still puzzling over the mysteries of Edgar Allan Poe and Arthur Conan Doyle

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: New Delhi, home to over 30 million people, regularly ranks among the world's most polluted areas during winter, with pollution worsening in late October and November.
articles.title: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution

articles.author: Kate Bartlett
articles.description: Russell Brand, who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, was found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in a case brought by six women.
articles.title: British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault

articles.author: Tess Ikonomou and Josh Butler
articles.description:
Government flags criminal law changes to ensure companies can’t argue in future ‘that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded’

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

OpenAI will not face criminal penalties over the Medicare data breach, but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.
Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia, but not the findings or the report itself, which he committed to releasing in the future.
Maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment.
Identifying and managing serious risks associated with their models.
Providing mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly.
Allowing independent evaluation of their models.
Maintaining and publishing safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency.
Responding to updated standards and rules as technologies change.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’

articles.author: Emma Graham-Harrison Chief Middle East correspondent
articles.description:
Opposition politicians get first chance to take control of levers of power, even as they struggle to form government
Israel’s new Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday, giving opposition politicians their first chance to take control of some levers of power, even as they struggle to form a new government to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu.
High on the agenda will be replacing the speaker, who wields immense influence by controlling the legislature’s agenda. The role is currently held by Amir Ohana, a close ally of Netanyahu.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New Knesset speaker could be key to ousting Netanyahu as Israel’s PM

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll
articles.description:
Jens Eskelund says Europe may need to allow its companies to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains
Europe’s manufacturers could give up on attempting to compete with their Chinese counterparts by the end of the decade if current trends continue amid fears over mass job losses, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China has warned.
In a case of “if you can’t beat them, join them”, Jens Eskelund said European companies operating in China were now thinking “Made in China for China” could be replaced by a philosophy of “Made in China for the world”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: EU manufacturers could give up on competing with China by 2030, warns commerce chief

articles.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Iran war has fuelled energy price rise and clouded outlook, driving up unemployment, says Clare Lombardelli
Young people in Britain are bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” as employers hold back from hiring amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East, a deputy governor of the Bank of England has warned.
Clare Lombardelli, the Bank’s deputy governor for monetary policy, said the unfolding conflict, which has triggered a surge in energy prices and clouded the outlook for the economy, was contributing to an increase in youth unemployment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Young people in UK hit by ‘low-gear economy’, warns Bank of England deputy

articles.author: Kat Wong
articles.description:
Former police officer tells jury he joked about being ‘white girl crazy’ with friends as lawyer questions him about start of relationship with TV presenter

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied misusing his authority as a police officer to access CCTV footage of Jesse Baird or stalking him after their breakup, a court has heard.
But he admitted he entered Baird’s house while he wasn’t home to retrieve belongings, and ate an Easter egg he had bought for the television presenter.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon admits entering Jesse Baird’s house when he wasn’t home and eating Easter egg, murder trial hears

articles.author: Patrick Commins Economics editor
articles.description:
Westpac survey results signal growing sense of ‘helplessness’ while Jim Chalmers faces growing pressure to rein in spending
Confidence among mortgaged households has crashed to its lowest level in more than three decades amid a growing sense of “helplessness” about the economy, even as a dramatic shift in financial markets suggests there is now a strong chance of a Reserve Bank rate cut by this time next year.
The latest Westpac survey showed its consumer sentiment index sinking again in November to reach a four-year low, amid deepening pessimism about the near-term prospects for the economy.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mortgage holders’ confidence crashes to lowest level since 1994 as year that ‘feels like a recession’ looms

articles.author: Andrew Roth in Washington
articles.description:
First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe
US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.
The talks are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as Abu Dhabi talks begin

articles.author: Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
Inquiry recommends police investigate allegations of sexual assault and other abuse at Redeemer Baptist school

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An investigation into a private religious school accused of sexual, physical, psychological, spiritual and financial abuse has recommended it be barred from enrolling new students.
Former students and teachers of western Sydney’s Redeemer Baptist school told a New South Wales parliamentary inquiry about a string of disturbing allegations.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sydney private school accused of sexual abuse should be banned from enrolling new students, inquiry says

articles.author: Henry Belot
articles.description:
Party disendorses Preston candidate Franco Guardiani after social media posts emerge

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One Nation Victoria has disendorsed a candidate whose private social media account described Adolf Hitler as the “GOAT” and claimed that “importing Islam is making pedophilia legal”.
In a now-deleted social media post, the party’s candidate for Preston, Franco Guardiani, commented on a social media post on X asking people to: “Describe Hitler in one word? Be brutally honest.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: One Nation dumps Victorian election candidate who praised Adolf Hitler as ‘GOAT’

articles.author: Cecilia Nowell, Shrai Popat, Anna Betts and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Republican Thomas Massie moves to force vote to impeach Pete Hegseth

Sign up for US Breaking News email

Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, currently the House minority leader who is poised to become new Speaker next year, told CBS News that the Trump administration will hold a closed-door congressional briefing today to discuss Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Last week the Republican chairs of three key House committees also called on Huang to appear before lawmakers in a closed-door hearing on 18 November.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Donald Trump doubles down on defense of Pete Hegseth and attacks fresh effort to impeach him – as it happened

articles.author: Dara Kerr
articles.description:
Campaign over Prop 40, as measure was known, was most expensive in state history, flush with Silicon Valley dollars
California billionaires won a contentious ballot measure campaign, defeating a proposed one-time tax on their wealth.
The bruising campaign over Proposition 40 was the most expensive in state history and witness to back-and-forth dealing from tech billionaires and democratic leaders, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, who steadfastly opposed the measure. While supporters of Prop 40 cast it as a solution to drastic healthcare cuts from Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents led by prosperous billionaires mounted an influential campaign saying the billionaire tax was instead “an everyone tax”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: California voters fail to pass proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth

articles.author: Hilary Beaumont
articles.description:
Key environmental groups come out against bipartisan Baaja bill over fears it could spur datacenters and ICE jails
The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.
It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Senate advances bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy

articles.author: Abené Clayton
articles.description:
Runners seek medical treatment as 13-mile race held amid unusually high November temperatures
Police in southern California are investigating the circumstances that led to the hospitalization of nearly 30 runners who participated in the Santa Barbara Half on Sunday.
Santa Barbara police said in a statement to the Associated Press that they had opened an investigation after receiving reports from Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital about multiple half-marathon participants seeking medical treatment for “unusual symptoms”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police investigate as nearly 30 Santa Barbara half-marathon runners fall ill with ‘unusual symptoms’

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Chamber voted 73-25 to formally take up bill that will shorten timelines to start energy and datacenter projects
The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.
The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now face years-long delays in getting to the grid.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Senate advances bill to speed up permit reviews for infrastructure projects

articles.author: Sally Weale Education correspondent
articles.description:
Almost two-thirds of school leaders polled say new regime is much more intense than previous framework
More than half of headteachers in England who were polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are considering cutting short their careers as a result of the experience.
In response to the question “Has the inspection affected how long you intend to stay in your role?”, 52% of those who responded said they were thinking of leaving their job sooner than planned.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Headteachers consider leaving jobs earlier than planned after new Ofsted inspection

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Former builder got his big break after restoring the home of a producer who was working on a precursor to the show 
Tommy Walsh, the building and DIY expert who appeared on television shows including Ground Force, has died aged 69 after a long illness.
Walsh started his career as a professional builder before rising to fame alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock on the popular BBC garden makeover show from 1997 to 2005.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tommy Walsh, co-presenter of BBC’s Ground Force, dies aged 69

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
‘Not particularly complex’ defrosting hack has been attributed to Iran, with presumption it is linked to others across Europe
Iranian hackers like to send a message.
In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers has geopolitical context

articles.author: Emine Sinmaz and Kevin Rawlinson
articles.description:
TV producer, who was in relationship with ex-comedian that reportedly ended in 2014, accuses him of ‘violence, coercive control and abuse’  

Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault

Jemima Goldsmith has said Russell Brand physically assaulted her and she accused him of “violence, coercive control and abuse”.
The 52-year-old TV producer said she has always been “strongly and unequivocally” on the side of Brand’s victims as she opened up about her own “painful” experience with her former partner in a social media post on Monday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jemima Goldsmith says ex-partner Russell Brand physically assaulted her

articles.author: Matthew Pearce
articles.description:
Particles from fireworks and bonfires likely to have contributed to levels well above WHO’s daily guideline
Air pollution soared to “very high” levels across urban parts of England on Monday as still, foggy weather kept emissions trapped after a weekend of fireworks and bonfires.
Government monitoring showed 11 sites, mainly in London and Greater Manchester, reached the highest band on its 10-point index for particulate matter in the 24 hours to 10am. A further 27 sites recorded “high” levels across the capital, the north-west, the Midlands, Yorkshire and the east of England.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Air pollution soars as fog traps emissions in England’s urban areas

articles.author: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke
articles.description:
High winds and heavy train triggered collapse of sand bank overlooking camp for displaced families
Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a landslide triggered by high winds and heavy rain in Gaza.
A sand bank overlooking a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah collapsed on Sunday, killing five people and crushing at least three tents.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Witnesses recount struggle to save people buried in ‘horrifying’ Gaza landslide

articles.author: Kim Willsher in Paris
articles.description:
French foreign minister vows European sanctions against Tehran over ‘unprecedented’ hacks last month
France has said Iran was responsible for a massive cyber-attack on supermarket freezers and chiller cabinets that was described by its foreign minister as being an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression”.
Jean-Noël Barrot said “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible, adding that the attacks – which took control of digital thermostats to push temperatures up to above 50C – constituted “a major violation of the nation’s interests”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran was behind cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers, Paris says

articles.author: Ashifa Kassam
articles.description:
Five-times Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner says he is neither leftwing nor rightwing but would seek to ‘bring people together’
The French judo star and five-times Olympic gold medallist Teddy Riner has announced plans to run in next year’s presidential election, describing himself as someone neither leftwing nor rightwing but who would seek to “bring people together”.
With more than five months before the April-May ballot to replace Emmanuel Macron, the race has been shaping up to be a showdown between political extremes. Polls point to a hollowing out of the political centre, suggesting that the anti-immigrant National Rally leader Marine Le Pen could be the frontrunner, with the radical-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon trailing behind.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I know what it’s like to fight’- France’s most popular sportsman says he’s running for president

articles.author: Oliver Wyndham-Lewis and Magdalena Shopova for the MetDesk
articles.description:
Violent storms lash northern Iraq and parts of Iran, while Portugal faces strong winds and Japan braces for further snowfall
Deadly flash floods hit northern Iraq on Saturday as severe thunderstorms swept across the region, including in neighbouring Iran. The city of Erbil, in Iraq, was particularly badly hit, with extensive damage to homes and businesses. Streets were inundated as torrential rain fell over a short period.
Rainfall exceeded forecasts, with an estimated 80mm falling in the city, compared with expectations of 30mm. Two people were killed in the floods.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Deadly floods hit Iraq as thunderstorms sweep across region

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
Pontiff tells Argentina’s president the economy must benefit all on second stop of 12-day Latin America tour
Pope Leo XIV has delivered a stinging critique of Argentine president Javier Milei’s harsh austerity measures, insisting growth must benefit all in a speech met with rapturous applause in Buenos Aires.
“The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy,” he said on Sunday, shortly after landing in Argentina on the second leg of a Latin America tour.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pope Leo delivers stinging rebuke of Milei’s austerity measures during Argentina visit

articles.author: Marina Dunbar and Robert Mackey
articles.description:
CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nvidia opens investigation after report CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign intelligence

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Former military chief says prime minister brought Israel to historic crisis and it is approaching ‘point of no return’
Israel’s former military chief Gadi Eisenkot started the tough task of forming a government on Sunday, reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu’s allies as he said the veteran prime minister had brought the country to a historic crisis.
Eisenkot, 66, the leader of the Yashar party, who has vowed to bridge Israel’s deep polarisation under Netanyahu, formally received a mandate from the president, Isaac Herzog, who gave him 28 days to form a government despite his bloc lacking a clear majority.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Gadi Eisenkot reaches out to Netanyahu allies as he strives to form government

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Knesset has been deadlocked since the election last month when Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority
Israel’s president has ⁠chosen Gadi Eisenkot, the prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ⁠strongest rival, to ⁠try to ​form a new government, after a deadlocked election that left neither man ⁠with a clear path to power.
Isaac Herzog’s office said he had informed Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, on Saturday night “of his intention to task him with forming a government”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israel’s president picks Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to form government

articles.author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester

articles.author: Facundo Iglesia in Buenos Aires
articles.description:
President has opposing views on many issues, and once called Leo’s predecessor the ‘representative of the Evil One’
Trees are being planted in the garden. The brightly coloured buildings are getting another coat of paint. The choir rehearses. Hundreds of other residents, several of them using wheelchairs, practise their positions outside the sanctuary. Excitement is in the air, because on Monday 9 November, the Cottolengo Don Orione – a Catholic-run home for disabled people – will be the first stop on Pope Leo XIV’s first full day of his trip to Argentina.
But the pope’s visit to Claypole, about 26km from Buenos Aires, does not come at an especially happy time for the home, which counts about 400 residents with disabilities. Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has made wide-ranging cuts to disability funding.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pope’s visit to Argentina sets up showdown with ‘hyper-capitalist’ Milei

articles.author: Sarah Butler
articles.description:
Farmers face big drop in production from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event
Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event.
High winds in parts of Colombia, one of the biggest suppliers to the UK market where droughts are predicted in some regions this year, and heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador are already affecting production, according to the Fairtrade Foundation ethical trade body. In the Dominican Republic, farmers are expected to face drought conditions, with forecasts of drier and warmer than usual conditions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Banana producers in Latin America want better pay to cope with effects of climate crisis

articles.author: Rebecca Ratcliffe, Gloria Dickie and Elisângela Mendonça
articles.description:
Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo
The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.
A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm

articles.author: Amy Hawkins
articles.description:
Activists fear Bangkok will give in to pressure from Beijing despite reports of torture and human rights abuses against the mostly muslim ethnic minority
The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN.
 

 

 The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Uyghurs facing deportation by Thailand say they will be ‘like slaves’ in China

articles.author: Eva Corlett in Auckland
articles.description:
National party will be largest in parliament but ultimate shape of next government won’t be settled for some time
New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.
On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NZ election 2026: New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with results ‘too close to call’

articles.author: Mark Saunokonoko
articles.description:
This blog is closed, you can read our report on the New Zealand election here

Another update here with 8% of the vote counted.
 

 

 National on 31.2%, Labour 28.4%, the Greens 12.9%, Act 11.2%, NZ First 9.6%, Opportunity 5.7% and Te Pāti Māori 0.4%.
On these numbers, we would have a right bloc coalition back in power. Long way to go.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New Zealand election coalition talks will likely take weeks – as it happened

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Department had claimed that being kidnapped for ransom was not exploitation of trafficking victims in case of Syrian man abducted in Libya
The court of appeal has rejected claims by the Home Office that being kidnapped for ransom is not exploitation of trafficking victims.
The ruling means that many people who have been kidnapped for ransom, whom officials have previously excluded from being victims of exploitation under trafficking rules, will now have to have these claims considered. They may be eligible for the support and recovery package trafficking victims are entitled to.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Court rules against Home Office in asylum seeker kidnapping case

articles.author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
articles.description:
Santiago Peña was detained minutes after he was impeached by Congress, as protesters took to the streets demanding answers after the suspension of the Ueno bank
Paraguay’s rightwing president has been placed under house arrest minutes after he was impeached by Congress, amid a severe crisis that left more than half the country’s population unable to access their bank accounts.
Santiago Peña is being investigated about allegations he used his political influence to favour a bank that expanded exponentially under his government and was suspended this week after irregularities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ousted Paraguay president under house arrest after banking crisis leaves 60% of country unable to access accounts

articles.author: Mark Sweney and Graeme Wearden
articles.description:
Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come
European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier.
A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Global stocks fall amid ‘big worries over AI’ after Democrats’ midterms triumph

articles.author: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies
articles.description:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result
The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted

articles.author: Sarah Johnson
articles.description:
Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.
“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final years

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’

articles.author: Patrick Greenfield, Elisângela Mendonça and Phoebe Weston and Spoorthy Raman
articles.description:
Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of  Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal imports

British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.
This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK ministers told not to engage formally with Indian mega-zoo after lobbying

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Led by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter roll
Thousands of opposition supporters have gathered in Delhi as protests against the Narendra Modi government continue to gather momentum.
Led by the Congress party, India’s opposition alliance has brought together supporters from across the country, amid growing anger over a large-scale revision of the country’s voter roll that has seen 130 million names erased.
 Continue reading...

articles.author: Jonathan Liew
articles.description:
Democrats won seats on anti-datacentre tickets and Musk wasted nearly half a billion dollars. Big tech may be losing its grip, but it won’t go quietly
Photos That Precede Unfortunate Events: a couple of months back, Donald Trump hosted some of the world’s most powerful tech executives at the White House for a “Super Intelligence luncheon”, which by coincidence is also how my mum described her tuna sandwiches in a forlorn attempt to get me to eat them. Sitting either side of the president were Elon Musk, making a rare offline appearance in daylight hours, and Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive carving out a precious slot in what we now know was an extremely busy schedule.
Over a delicious meal of microchips and rare-earth metals, the billionaires sketched out a utopian future of an AI industry unencumbered by regulation or safeguards, powered by their heroic strongman leader, a political genius effortlessly able to impose his will upon an entire nation. And perhaps it should have been apparent even at the time that these (mostly) men were putting their faith in a guy who had recently been defeated by pond algae. But as the drinks and the good times flowed, it was still possible to believe that the sun would never set on the thousand-year American superintelligence empire.
Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

His disdain for Europe and his evident delight in attacking its governments – in particular that of Ukraine – have been hard to swallow.
Relief, because the midterm election results confirm that Europeans are not unique in being appalled by Trump’s actions: a large majority of Americans are too. And like many Americans, in these results Europeans see hope that US democracy can be saved, American foreign policy moderated and the transatlantic partnership revived.

The home secretary has hailed the expanded use of immigration enforcement teams, and claimed they will help to secure the UK’s borders by removing a key incentive for irregular migration.
There were 23,538 immigration enforcement engagements such as workplace raids, home raids and spot checks in 2025 – or 60 a day. Of these, 15,578, or 66.1%, resulted in no arrests.
Only 25.81% of visits where a premises was accessed used a warrant. Critics say this suggests the Home Office is launching “fishing expeditions” based on weak intelligence.
Nearly nine out of 10 (89%) of leads alleging “immigration crime” in 2025 came from the public or from Crimestoppers, a charity that collects anonymous tip-offs. Around 2% came from the police.

Physiotherapy services hit particularly hard compared with other areas of healthcare such as nursing, union finds
Almost half of the NHS trusts in England have no earmarked funding to cover staff on maternity leave, according to analysis that raises fresh concerns about pressure on physiotherapy services.
Freedom of information requests sent to the trusts by the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy (CSP) found that 49% had neither a dedicated budget nor a policy to permit overspending to pay for maternity cover.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Half of NHS trusts in England lack funds earmarked to cover maternity leave

articles.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
articles.description:
Scheme in Derry aims to sow confidence by getting people with learning and physical disabilities into wrestling
The music thumped, the lights blazed and from the ring the announcer did a countdown. “Who is ready to rumble?” he roared. The bellows and cheers indicated that the crowd at St Columb’s Hall in Derry on Saturday night was more than ready for the Foyle Rumble, and so began a wrestling extravaganza of heroes and villains in leotards, masks and kneepads.
The blend of athleticism and scripted storytelling would have been familiar to fans of WrestleMania, but this Northern Irish version came with a twist: many of the performers have learning or physical disabilities, and the characters they play in the ring do not quite stay in the ring.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘No matter what, he doesn’t quit’: disabled wrestlers draw strength from ring alter egos

articles.author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
A lifestyle podcast or brief TV clip is less taxing than a full press conference – but No 10 insists the PM is not ducking accountability 
In an interview this week Andy Burnham said he believed the traditional media was less relevant and the world was “not like that any more”. But some people are now asking: does this change in approach mean less scrutiny?
The question was in part prompted by Burnham’s decision to travel to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) without the usual accompanying pack of reporters, instead bringing just one TV crew and a news agency journalist.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Does Andy Burnham’s pivot from press to social media put scrutiny at risk?

articles.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
articles.description:
Twelve midwife-led maternity units have closed in England since 2019 with six closing since Labour came to power in 2024
NHS officials are shutting growing numbers of birth centres in a “shocking” denial of a woman’s right to have a midwife rather than a doctor oversee their baby’s birth, say campaigners.
Twelve birth centres – midwife-led maternity units – have closed in England since 2019. Birth centres play a key role in ensuring that women can choose whether to have their baby at a unit in a hospital run by doctors, at one where midwives are in charge, or at home.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rise in NHS birth centre closures ‘shocking’ denial of women’s rights, experts say

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Charges against party members and off-piste remarks highlight problems brought about by rapid expansion
Speaking to reporters after unveiling his new defence spokesperson this week, Nigel Farage’s jovial and upbeat mood suddenly switched. Why, he was asked, was a Reform UK councillor who was arrested in January over multiple alleged sexual offences still in his role nearly 10 months later?
“I have no idea,” Farage replied icily. “I was told yesterday, and I wasn’t very happy.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Vetting candidates is a tricky process but Reform can’t seem to get it right

articles.author: Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Nesrine Malik, produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke John Smith, the executive producers were Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale
articles.description:
Today’s political conversation is dominated by one topic above all: race. The Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik has been way ahead of the pack in diagnosing how immigrants, their children and grandchildren are reshaping not just politics but western societies. On the latest episode of Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty, Nesrine talks about where never-ending culture wars in the west and real wars in the Middle East have left people of colour.

Watch more episodes of Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty here
Aditya’s suggested reading list for Nesrine Malik:
In this podcast, Nesrine and I talk about how Gaza has reshaped politics in Britain and America. I quote from this column by her from November 2023 and also cite this prescient piece on Gaza and Labour, from October 2023.
We also discuss “identity politics” (a term only ever used against ethnic minorities). Her book We Need New Stories: Challenging the Toxic Myths Behind Our Age of Discontent is worth revisiting.
More recently, she has addressed the obits being written for Woke 1.0.
Finally, we didn’t get a chance to discuss Sudan’s civil war, but Nesrine’s Long Read on the Khartoum in which she grew up is very powerful.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why Woke 2.0 is taking on Trump and establishment politics | Nesrine Malik | Radical Thinking podcast

articles.author: Vikram Dodd and Emine Sinmaz
articles.description:
Met police chief says ‘many more’ victims could come forward, as actor and comedian awaits sentencing 
Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward, with at least 10 more women suspected of having been attacked by the disgraced star.
Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women

articles.author: Ian Sample Science editor
articles.description:
The most enjoyable conversations strike a balance between exploring a topic and pulling in fresh ideas, study finds
As an early stab at rules for conversation, Cicero did a fine job: watch your tone, never look bored, never lose your temper and never ramble on, particularly about yourself, he advised.
Now scientists have followed in the great orator’s footsteps and discovered a telltale signature of an enjoyable chinwag. The secret of a mutually satisfying exchange is a healthy dose of pink noise, they say.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’

articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor
articles.description:
Lisa Nandy calls for whistleblowers to be protected and highlights bravery of women who came forward in case
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, has warned that Russell Brand’s conviction for rape and sexual assault must be a “wake-up call” to the media world and beyond, after widespread concerns over the failures to confront his behaviour.
With renewed calls from TV insiders for a new examination of how Brand’s treatment of women was tolerated for so long, Nandy said the case was a “defining moment for our country”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russell Brand rape conviction must be ‘wake-up call’, says culture secretary

articles.author: Chris Osuh, Aamna Mohdin and Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Some relatives of British citizens say they feel left behind, but announcement has brought relief to many care workers
“The only time we’re regarded as human beings is when they need a lot of hands onboard, like during Covid. But after that, we’re tossed away like we’re some rubbish,” Aneisha Williams says.
Williams, 39, was months from qualifying for indefinite leave to remain after 10 years in the UK. But claiming housing benefit could delay her settlement for years under Shabana Mahmood’s “earned settlement” plans.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I feel free now’: Shabana Mahmood’s immigration shake-up provokes mixed emotions

articles.author: Pippa Neill
articles.description:
Mild autumn temperatures causing premature flowering and raising concerns for pollinators, say experts
Trees are experiencing an “early spring” because of mild UK temperatures this autumn, with experts warning this could cause long-term harm to pollinators.
Last month was warmer than average across all parts of the UK, with October marking the ninth consecutive month with above-average mean temperatures.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Everything is so out of whack’: UK trees experience spring six months early

articles.author: Presented by Nosheen Iqbal with Emine Sinmaz; produced by Saskia Collette and May Robson; executive producer Homa Khaleeli
articles.description:
In the decades he’s spent on screens, Russell Brand’s been a comedian, an actor, a presenter and a political anarchist.
Now he has been convicted of rape and sexual assaults.
Emine Sinmaz reports
We’ve seen many iterations of Russell Brand. Camp Camden goth. Outrageous standup and TV host. Hollywood star. Political anarchist. Reborn Christian conspiracy theorist.
Brand always wanted to be famous. And when he attained celebrity in the 2000s, he was seen as a breath of fresh air. Hyper-camp, hyper-sexual, hyper-articulate, he was considered edgy by TV and radio commissioners and funnier than anyone else by his fans. A Guardian columnist and the Sun’s shagger of the year, Brand was supposed to be ironic, a pop culture provocateur, journalist Sophie Heawood tells Nosheen Iqbal. But in the past decade, it’s become harder to remember why he was so celebrated.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The crimes of Russell Brand - podcast

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Doctor who was helping response to outbreak in Africa taken to specialist isolation unit at Royal Free hospital
A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has returned to the UK for specialist treatment.
The patient, whose identity is unknown, was transported home on a medical evacuation flight, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday. They are now being cared for in a specialised high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, north London.
 
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British Ebola patient evacuated from DR Congo arrives at London hospital

articles.description:
Senior crown prosecutor David Roberts and Det Supt Andy Furphy, from the Met police, praised the 'extraordinary courage, resilience and determination' of Russell Brand’s victims. Brand has been found guilty of raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others over the course of five years of his showbusiness career


Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault

 Continue reading...
articles.title: 'Justice has been served' for Russell Brand's victims, prosecutor says – video

articles.author: Emine Sinmaz
articles.description:
Actor and comedian, 51, found guilty of raping a woman and assaulting three others

Flashbulbs, lies and victim blaming: how Russell Brand’s trial unfolded

The downfall of Russell Brand: from Big Brother and Hollywood to convicted rapist

Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women, ending a years-long legal saga that has raised questions about how he was able to commit his crimes at the height of his fame.
Brand, 51, was described during his trial as a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator. He was convicted of raping a woman at his luxury London townhouse and of sexually assaulting women in front of his entourage at their workplaces, at a radio station and TV studio.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russell Brand faces ‘significant’ prison term for rape and sexual assault

articles.author: Rupert Jones
articles.description:
First rate rise for more than three years leaves millions facing rise in mortgage payments

Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%

Business live – latest updates

The Bank of England has hiked interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, taking the base rate to 4%. It is the first rate rise for more than three years, leaving millions of households facing a sharp rise in mortgage payments.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What does the UK interest rate rise mean for homeowners and savers?

articles.author: Sandra Laville
articles.description:
With parts of region served by company in severe drought still, regulators give it six weeks to come up with action plan
Repeated failures by South West Water to tackle leaks are putting customers at higher risks of losing water supplies as parts of the region remain in severe drought, regulators have said.
In a warning to the privatised company that serves 1.8 million people across the south-west of England, the regulators said it had been failing to meet targets to reduce leaks and repair burst pipes for seven years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South West Water’s failure to fix leaks ‘putting customer supplies at risk’

articles.author: Karen McVeigh
articles.description:
Four-year study warns destabilised marine food webs could jeopardise food security by 2050
Warming seas around the UK and the wider north-east Atlantic could destabilise marine food webs, weaken ocean health and jeopardise food security by 2050, according to a four-year study.
Scientists who projected the impact of climate breakdown on four key groups of marine life crucial to maintaining ocean ecosystems in the region said their results challenged assumptions that in middle latitudes, such as the UK, marine biodiversity was likely to increase across the board.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Warming UK seas could ‘fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems’ – report

articles.description:
King Charles addressed country leaders at the opening ceremony of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting, calling the transatlantic slave trade a 'shameful chapter of history … that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow'. Speaking in Antigua and Barbuda, the king said the slave trade 'still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth', but his remarks stopped short of an apology. Charles spoke just days after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he was open to making a formal apology, although he has rejected calls for the UK to pay reparations


King Charles addresses summit as campaigners intensify demands for apology for slavery

 Continue reading...
articles.title: 'Shameful chapter': King Charles stops short of slavery apology in Commonwealth speech – video

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
With heir apparent Danny Tommo also in custody, Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists is blow to anti-migrant movement
The verdict was met with a groan from Tommy Robinson’s supporters, who had sat behind the dock throughout his harassment trial.
It took more than 11 hours of jury deliberations to find the far-right activist guilty of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists, enough time for a band of lieutenants and hangers-on to get their hopes up that he might be acquitted.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tommy Robinson conviction leaves far right with leadership void

articles.author: Tess Ikonomou and Josh Butler
articles.description:
Government flags criminal law changes to ensure companies can’t argue in future ‘that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded’

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

OpenAI will not face criminal penalties over the Medicare data breach, but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.
Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia, but not the findings or the report itself, which he committed to releasing in the future.
Maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment.
Identifying and managing serious risks associated with their models.
Providing mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly.
Allowing independent evaluation of their models.
Maintaining and publishing safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency.
Responding to updated standards and rules as technologies change.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.description:
Australia's prime minister said its government would set up a new AI safety regulator and Labor would consider six key obligations on AI companies. The review made 18 recommendations. Anthony Albanese said: 'We accept all of the recommendations, and we’ve commenced work to implement them.'

Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mandatory AI safety and security protections announced after OpenAI breach of Medicare – video

articles.description:
Donald Trump defended defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who is facing an impeachment resolution from Republican senator Thomas Massie, saying Hegseth 'won two wars'.  The president, who said he had spoken to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, said he was 'amazed' by claims Huang conducted an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and that the FBI was now looking into the issue

Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?

Republican Thomas Massie moves to force vote to impeach Pete Hegseth

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump backs embattled Hegseth and Jensen Huang and says FBI looking into spy allegations – video

articles.author: Jonathan Barrett Business editor
articles.description:
Australian carrier announces agreement with Accenture amid ‘unprecedented’ technological disruption, CEO Vanessa Hudson says

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Qantas is preparing to cut 850 local jobs and outsource work offshore under an AI-driven overhaul, marking a growing wave of disruption to the Australian workforce.
The changes represent the third major corporate layoff plan announced in Australia in three weeks, after restructuring moves flagged by the design company Canva and National Australia Bank.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Qantas to cut 850 Australian jobs and outsource work to India under AI-driven overhaul

articles.author: Nick Robins-Early
articles.description:
Elon Musk and other finance moguls defend Jensen Huang after he admitted to the affair, as Trump says FBI ‘is looking into it’ 

Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish

Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump said he has spoken to Huang on Monday as the scandal reverberated across Silicon Valley and the Nvidia CEO faced an uncertain future.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Silicon Valley and Trump rally behind Nvidia CEO after his affair with alleged Chinese spy

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision
For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large.
He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
‘Not particularly complex’ defrosting hack has been attributed to Iran, with presumption it is linked to others across Europe
Iranian hackers like to send a message.
In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers has geopolitical context

articles.author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
articles.description:
Exclusive: WhatsApp messages show firm pressuring Zubir Ahmed MP to help bring sensitive data into its platform

UK politics live – latest updates

Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients.
The US company, co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel, used a direct WhatsApp channel to argue that “the logic of joining up primary and secondary [care] data is unarguable” and said its software was “ideal” for the job. The push came in February this year despite GP data being expressly ruled out of the scope of Palantir’s existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform (FDP), which it says has helped cut surgery waiting times and discharge delays.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records

articles.author: Nils Pratley
articles.description:
The chipmaker faces business risks and political scrutiny due to its over-reliance on founder and CEO Jensen Huang

Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China row?

Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal. The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power.
Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish | Nils Pratley

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
Company says schools should control student AI use, but if they block its AI tools, they’ll lose access to search engine
Parents and teachers across the US are criticizing Google’s announcement that schools choosing to block AI tools could also lose access to Google Search.
Google announced last week a range of new AI tools for schools and classrooms, alongside options allowing teachers and administrators to restrict their use. The company said schools should have control over whether students use AI in the classroom, but that schools that choose to block Google’s AI tools will also lose access to its search engine.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Parents and teachers decry Google pledge to yank Search if schools block AI: ‘This threat is nothing but extortion’

articles.author: Sunita Verma
articles.description:
The same technical limits that prevent superintelligence make these systems dangerous. But we know how to regulate them
Many Silicon Valley leaders believe superintelligence is an imminent threat to society. The White House even published an accord about it. This isn’t enough.
Geoffrey Hinton, the godfather of AI, estimates the risk of human extinction is at least 10% within the next few decades. The Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, argued that unchecked AI “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems”. In response, 1,300 leaders and employees from many leading AI companies signed a letter calling to “deliberately pace” development.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Today’s AI won’t achieve superintelligence. But catastrophic risk is real | Sunita Verma

articles.author: Christian Donlan
articles.description:
Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art
In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them.
After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus

articles.author: Interview by Liam Pape
articles.description:
The writer and podcaster on why politics is made to seem more complicated than it is and his mission to unpack world events for everyone
Why did you get into comedy?
  
My mum was a professional dancer and always encouraged me to perform. Given that I have zero rhythm, comedy was my other option. She wrote me a poem called Mrs Brown’s Moggy, about a cat that was often very soggy, for my school’s talent show. Because you can’t tell the difference between real and polite laughter at the age of six, I assumed I’d killed my first gig and convinced myself I was born to do nothing else.
Where do you find your material?
  
In a world where Robert Jenrick claims Nigel Farage has “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism”, the answer is that my material is presented to me on a silver platter each morning.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Thicky thicky dumb dumb’ satirist Cody Dahler on his viral videos: ‘my material is presented to me on a silver platter!’

articles.author: Kiran Stacey Policy editor
articles.description:
Exclusive: Louise Haigh likely to weaken mandate for sales that forms key part of emission reduction plan

Analysis: Climate always comes second – are green issues slipping down Burnham’s agenda?

Ministers are expected to make steep cuts to the government’s electric vehicle (EV) targets this week, in a move that will relieve carmakers but alarm many Labour MPs who are worried about the government’s commitment to the green agenda.
Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, will finalise the plan after a crunch meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday to settle a long-running dispute between the transport, energy and business departments.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Labour expected to cut EV targets for UK’s car industry despite MPs’ protests

articles.author: Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend
articles.description:
From roundabouts to the stock market, relentless streamlining could be making the world more dangerous
We have all been there: packed shoulder to shoulder on the train while the person beside us coughs and sneezes. A protective flu jab offers some reassurance, but so does the thought that there will be a hospital bed for you, should you need it. Yet, in England, about 95% of adult hospital beds were occupied at the height of flu season last year.
If hospitals were hotels, that level of occupancy would be good business, and we would commend them for their efficiency. But do we really want a hospital to have so few beds in reserve that it’s just one bad flu week away from having to treat patients in corridors?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly

articles.author: Joanna Partridge
articles.description:
MPs, local authorities, lawyers, schools and more are receiving floods of grievances, requests and legal challenges, often complex to read and respond to
‘It started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence.
“Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” she says, adding that this has made requests and complaints much more complex and time-consuming to read and deal with, despite her decade of experience in the role. “It is definitely more taxing.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints

articles.author: Dan Milmo and Aisha Down
articles.description:
As AI exposes flaws in IT systems and geopolitics plays out on the cyber frontline, some experts say the events of recent weeks could soon be a common occurrence
Alex Pearce was doing the morning rounds at his fruit and vegetable wholesale business in London on Monday last week when he noticed something odd.
The defrost light on refrigeration unit 2 was on, and the panel reading was 150C. Unit 4 was the same.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?

articles.author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
articles.description:
In a war driven by drones and battlefield sensors, access to space is essential. After Starlink speed restrictions and Russian Oreshnik missile strikes, Kyiv is racing to develop its own space capabilities
For people in the Russian industrial city of Samara on the banks of the Volga, the first they knew of the Ukrainian attack were detonations that sent a column of smoke into the air.
If the Kremlin was vague about the target, video footage on social media soon made it clear what had been hit in the early hours of 15 August: the Progress Rocket and Space Centre, manufacturer of Russia’s Soyuz-2 rockets.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ukraine’s new frontier: how space has become critical to balance of the war

articles.author: Zoe Wood
articles.description:
Fans trying to access latest releases are being priced out in a cut-throat market driven by crypto-like hype
The runaway demand for Pokemon cards is because they are being hyped “like crypto”, according to one young fan who had spent the night queueing outside a London store to make sure he did not miss out on the latest card release.
Before its 10am opening on Friday, the line outside the pop culture store Forbidden Planet in central London snaked past five others and, despite its strict sales policy, was probably “50/50” fans and resellers, said Kai, who had been there since 3am.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Gotta buy ’em all: how Pokémon card collecting became race against scalpers

articles.author: Tom Regan
articles.description:
When our writer found himself among the hundreds on Oxford Street hoping to get their hands on early copies and collectibles, it was a heartwarming reminder of the shared experience of fandom
• The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
It is Thursday night and I am sat blurry-eyed and runny nosed outside the Argos on Oxford Street. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills.
These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. But in a bygone era, when we used to go to shops to buy games, midnight launches offered a space for likeminded enthusiasts to gather and celebrate their fandom. Every Call of Duty, Halo or Grand Theft Auto release would have fans queueing outside branches of Game or Electronics Boutique, many dressed as favourite characters.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.description:
As GTA 6 looms, we look at the films that have influenced Rockstar’s creatives, from Heat to Bonnie and Clyde, via Boyz n the Hood and Speed
Grand Theft Auto is arguably the most cinematic video game series ever made. Over the past three decades, the games have studied and stolen the themes, conventions and visual dynamism of great gangster and action movies, applying them to open worlds filled with low-life characters and grand set-piece possibilities. Here then are the movies (and TV show) that have shaped the GTA experience, from the 1996 original to this year’s inescapable instalment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto

articles.author: Blake Montgomery
articles.description:
Democrats’ success was helped by popular anger over tech, AI and the super rich – life for billionaires could become much more difficult
The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires.
The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tech barons cozied up to Trump. What will they do in newly blue America?

articles.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor

articles.description:
Titanium Court is a bizarre world of 8-bit fairies, Shakespeare and surprise songs – its magic lies in never knowing what on earth is going on
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
Earlier this year, I was stuck in hospital for several days, fuzzy on pain medication and bored out of my mind, with nothing but a Steam Deck for company. In the middle of one of those long nights, unable to sleep, I played a game called Titanium Court. It’s a strange creation that looks like it was made for the ZX Spectrum and reads like a postmodern Shakespeare adaptation – a compelling mix of strategy game and match-3 where you rearrange battlefields by matching tiles, before sending tiny lo-fi fairy armies to their deaths.
At the end of this late-night run, I met a boss I’d defeated before – a comically hungry dragon – and the game asked if I would like to skip the boss fight and enjoy a musical performance instead. A game has never asked me this before. Of course, I accepted. And then, instead of the familiar tiled battlefield, I was looking at a pixellated singer-songwriter, who launched into an extremely long preamble about the mating habits of the Pacific salmon before saying, “This is a song for anyone else who ever got so horny they could die,” and launching into a soulful acoustic guitar number accompanied by crude images of leaping fish. I began to wonder if my meds were making me hallucinate.

articles.title: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites
